uncited: Computes the view and perspective projection matrices for an arcball-style camera, handling rotation around a pivot point and avoiding pitch flip artifacts.

It differs from standard look-at methods by explicitly managing the camera position via sequential yaw and pitch rotations around a fixed target, ensuring the view direction remains well-defined even at extreme angles.
- Camera position ($P$), target ($T$), and up vector ($U$).
- Screen aspect ratio ($w/h$), vertical field of view ($\phi$), near plane ($z_{near}$), and far plane ($z_{far}$).
- Rotation matrices are constructed from axis-angle representation.
**Compute View Direction:** Calculate the normalized vector from the target to the current position: $V = \text{normalize}(P - T)$.
**Gimbal Lock Check:** Compute the dot product $d = V \cdot U$.
**Yaw Rotation:** Rotate the position $P$ around the pivot $C$ by $\theta_{yaw}$ using $U$ as the rotation axis.
**Pitch Rotation:** Rotate $P_{yaw}$ around the pivot $C$ by $\theta_{pitch}$ using $R_{vec}$ as the rotation axis.
Matrix multiplications and vector operations are constant time for fixed-size matrices.
Stores only the camera state and two 4x4 matrices.
Provides intuitive control for orbiting around a target.
- **Limitations:** Not suitable for first-person cameras where the up vector should remain fixed relative to the world or camera.
The pitch flip check is a heuristic (0.99 threshold) and may not cover all edge cases.
- **When to use:** Interactive 3D viewers, orbit cameras, and applications where the camera rotates around a central object.
- **When not to use:** First-person shooters, flight simulators, or any application requiring continuous pitch rotation without limits.
It allows users to rotate objects by dragging on a virtual sphere.
